DISJOINT NON-FORKING AMALGAMATION IN STABLE AECS
JEREMY BEARD
Abstract. The disjoint amalgamation property (DAP), which asserts that
all spans of a class of models can be amalgamated with minimal intersection,
is an important property in the context of abstract elementary classes, with
connections to both Grossberg’s question [She01, Problem (5)] and Shelah’s
categoricity conjecture [She00, Question 6.14(3)].
We prove that, in a nice
AEC K stable in λ ≥LS(K) with a strong enough independence relation, all
high cofinality λ-limit models are disjoint (non-forking) amalgamation bases.
Theorem 3.1. Let K be an AEC stable in λ, where Kλ has AP, JEP, and
NMM, and let K′ be some AC where K(λ,≥κ) ⊆K′ ⊆Kλ.
Let ⌣be
an independence relation on K′ satisfying uniqueness, existence, non-forking
amalgamation, K(λ,≥κ)-universal continuity* in Kλ, and (≥κ)-local charac-
ter.
Assume M0, M1, M2 ∈K(λ,≥κ), and that M0 ≤K Ml and al ∈Ml for
l = 1, 2. Then there exist N ∈K(λ,≥κ) and fl : Ml →N fixing M0 for l = 1, 2
such that gtp(fl(al)/f3−l[M3−l], N) ⌣-does not fork over M0 and f1[M1] ∩
f2[M2] = M0. That is, ⌣↾K(λ,≥κ) has disjoint non-forking amalgamation.
In particular, every M0 ∈K(λ,≥κ) is a disjoint amalgamation base in Kλ.
The hypotheses on the independence relation can be weakened (closer to
λ-non-splitting in λ-stable AECs) if we are willing to give up the ‘non-forking’
conditions of the amalgamation.
This generalises [Vas19, Lemma 5.36], which applied only to categorical
AECs, and more broadly continues the current effort to explore the structure
of strictly stable abstract elementary classes.
1. Introduction
In the context of abstract elementary classes (AECs), the disjoint amalgamation
property (DAP) is an important notion with connections to some of the central open
problems in AECs, such as Grossberg’s question [She01, Problem (5)] (e.g. [Gro,
Lemma 2.4.10]) and Shelah’s categoricity conjecture [She00, Question 6.14(3)] (e.g.
[Vas19, Fact 6.2]). Given an AEC (or more generally an abstract class) K, we say
M ∈K is a disjoint amalgamation base in K if for any two K-extensions M1, M2
of M where M1 and M2 have the same cardinality as M, there exist K-embeddings
fl : Ml →N fixing M such that f1[M1] ∩f2[M2] = M; that is, the intersection is
the minimal possible one. We say a subclass K′ ⊆K has disjoint amalgamation in
K or DAP in K if every M ∈K′ is a disjoint amalgamation base in K. In the case
K = K′, we simply say K has disjoint amalgamation or DAP.
Given a first order complete theory T, the class of models of T with elementary
embeddings has DAP by an application of Robinson’s Consistency Lemma [Gro,
Corollary 4.2.10].
However, in the more general setting of AECs, it is possible
for DAP to fail, even assuming the amalgamation property (see Example 2.4). In
this paper, we show that if a nice AEC K which is stable in some λ ≥LS(K)

In fact, the joint embedding property and no maximal models assumptions are
unnecessary (see Remark 3.32).
The argument hinges on the theory of towers developed in [BeMa, §3]. Towers
are essentially sequences of high cofinality limit models with named elements (see
Definition 2.27). An ordering ◁on towers can be defined (see 2.30), which demands
the singletons of towers have nice non-forking properties over the lesser towers.
Of particular importance to us are reduced towers - these are towers which have
minimal intersections with the models ◁-extending towers.
We approach the proof of Theorem 3.1 in stages, which we sketch here.
In
Subsection 3.1 we show that pairs of towers with the same bottom model can
themselves be amalgamated - that is, you can form a matrix of models where the
leftmost column and bottom row are isomorphic to two given towers, and the towers’
singletons have nice non-forking properties with the matrix. In Subsection 3.2 we
show how to build a reduced tower where the top model is a high cofinality limit
model over the bottom model. We put these together in Subsection 3.3: using that
high cofinality limit models are isomorphic (Fact 2.43), we can ensure that (using
the notation from the statement of Theorem 3.1) the bottom model of the tower is
M0, the top model is M1, and a1 is the bottom singleton of the tower. By applying
tower amalgamation to this constructed tower and the tower ⟨M0, M2⟩∧⟨a2⟩, we
get the desired non-forking amalgamation (the non-forking comes from the way
we amalgamated the towers in the first step). Further, the ‘minimal intersection’
condition of the reduced tower guarantees disjointness.

DISJOINT NON-FORKING AMALGAMATION IN STABLE AECS

This approach is loosely inspired by [Vas19, Lemma 5.36], where this disjoint
‘non-forking’ amalgamation is shown to hold for all models in an AEC which is
categorical in λ ≥LS(K) as well as being λ-superstable and λ-symmetric, and used
a specific independence relation called λ-non-forking. Theorem 3.1 has the advan-
tages of applying to strictly stable AECs, as well as using a general independence
notion rather than λ-non-forking. However, without the categoricity assumption,
we can only prove that (high cofinality) λ-limit models are disjoint (non-forking)
amalgamation bases, rather than all models of size λ.
In Subsection 3.4, we show that in a more general setting (where our inde-
pendence relation satisfies only ‘weak’ versions of uniqueness, extension, and non-
forking amalgamation, similar to λ-non-splitting in λ-stable AECs), all high co-
finality λ-limit models are disjoint amalgamation bases.
However, we have not
been able to show the non-forking of the amalgamation can be guaranteed. This
is because, in this context, we must use the notion of towers from [Bea25] (in this
paper called weak towers). These interact more fruitfully with the weaker forms
of uniqueness, extension, and non-forking amalgamation our independence relation
assumes, but are trickier to work with.
It remains open whether an analogous
disjoint non-forking amalgamation can be performed in this setting (see Question
3.31).
This paper is split into three sections. Section 2 provides the necessary back-
ground. In particular, the theory of towers is introduced - we only state the relevant
definitions and results, but an interested reader can consult [BeMa, §3] for a more
thorough introduction. Section 3 contains all new arguments - in particular, Sub-
sections 3.1, 3.2, and 3.3 together prove Theorem 3.1. Subsection 3.4 introduces
the theory of towers from [Bea25] which we call weak towers to distinguish from
those used in the rest of the paper, before proving the disjoint amalgamation result
in this weaker setting.
This paper was written while the author was working on a Ph.D. thesis under the
direction of Rami Grossberg at Carnegie Mellon University, and the author would
like to thank Professor Grossberg for his guidance and assistance in his research in
general and in this work specifically.
2. Preliminaries
We will extensively use material from [BeMa, §3], particularly the theory of
reduced and full towers, and the main result of that section ([BeMa, Theorem
3.1]). We present the relevant material in this section for the convenience of the
reader. A reader familiar with [BeMa, §3] can skip this section.
For now, we assume some background knowledge of abstract elementary classes
(AECs) - see for example [Bal09].
2.1. Basic notions, notations, and conventions. An abstract class (AC) is
a pair K = (K, ≤K) class of models K closed under isomorphisms, with a partial
order ≤K which strengthens the substructure relation ⊆and respects isomorphisms.
Often K will be an AEC. Given a model M, |M| denotes its universe, and ∥M∥
its cardinality. We use the standard abuses of notation M ∈K instead of M ∈K,
and sometimes use M in place of the universe |M|, e.g. a ∈M. M ∼= N signals
that the models M and N are isomorphic, and M ∼=
M0 N denotes that there is
an isomorphism from M to N fixing the common ≤K-substructure M0. We use

α, β, γ . . . to denote ordinals, often reserving δ for limits, λ for cardinals, and κ
for a regular cardinals. Given two sequences σ and τ, their concatenation is σ∧τ.
Given an AC K = (K, ≤K), we say K′ = (K′, ≤K′) is a sub-AC of K if K′ is an
AC, K′ ⊆K, and ≤K′=≤K↾(K′)2. When K is an AC and λ is a cardinal, Kλ is
the sub-AC of K with underlying class Kλ = {M ∈K : ∥M∥= λ} ordered by the
restriction of ≤K to Kλ. K≥λ and K≥λ are defined similarly. Given M ≤K N and
a ∈N, gtp(a/M, N) denotes the Galois type of a over M in N. The set of (1-ary)
Galois types over M is denoted gS(M). We say K is λ-stable if for all M ∈K with
∥M∥= λ, | gS(M)| ≤λ.
An AC K has the amalgamation property (AP) if for all M0, M1, M2 where
M0 ≤K Ml for l = 1, 2, there exist N and K-embeddings fl : Ml →N fixing M0
for l = 1, 2. K has the joint embedding property (JEP) if every two models M1 and
M2 have K-embeddings into a common structure N. K has no maximal models
(NMM) if for all M ∈K, there exists N ∈K where M <K N.
Definition 2.1. Let K be an AC. We say that M ∈K is a disjoint amalgamation
base in K if for every M1, M2 ∈K∥M∥such that M ≤K Ml for l = 1, 2, there exist
N and fl : Ml →N fixing M for l = 1, 2 such that f1[M1] ∩f2[M2] = M.
If K is clear from context, we may omit it.
If every M ∈K is a disjoint
amalgamation base, we say K satisfies the disjoint amalgamation property or DAP.
Compare this to the definition of the amalgamation property - disjoint amalga-
mation requires the extra ‘minimal intersection’ condition, but note disjoint amal-
gamation we only ask that our conclusion holds for models of the same cardinality.
Other authors may not enforce the cardinality condition, but since in this paper
we will only discuss AP and DAP holding in Kλ for an AC K and some cardinal
λ, the notions will be the same for our main results. In light of this, DAP can be
viewed as a stronger condition than AP.
In first order model theory, AP and DAP are actually equivalent by an appli-
cation of Robinson’s consistency lemma [Gro, Corollary 4.2.10]. However, in the
AEC setting DAP is strictly stronger than AP, since there exists a very nice AEC
satisfying AP (and JEP, NMM, and stability in all cardinals) which does not satisfy
the DAP in any cardinal (see Example 2.4).
DAP has a couple of alternative formulations.
Lemma 2.2. Let K be an AC, and M ∈K. Then M is a disjoint amalgamation
base if and only if for every M1, M2 ∈K∥M∥such that M ≤K Ml for l = 1, 2, there
exist N and fl : Ml →N for l = 1, 2 such that f1[M1] ∩f2[M2] = f[M].
Proof. It is clear if M is a disjoint amalgamation base, then any f1, f2 witnessing
this are sufficient.

let N and fl : Ml →N for l = 1, 2 be such that f1[M1] ∩f2[M2] = f[M]. Take

The following reformulation essentially says that, since the places where a disjoint

M1 ∩M2 = M0 already, we may assume M1 \ M0 and M2 \ M0 are fixed.

Lemma 2.3. Suppose K is an AC, and M0 ∈K. Then M0 is a disjoint amal-
gamation base if and only if whenever M1, M2 ∈K∥M0∥such that M0 ≤K Ml for
l = 1, 2 and M1 ∩M2 = M0, then there exists N ∈K such that M1, M2 ≤K N.
Proof. The reverse implication is trivial, so suppose M0 is an amalgamation base.
Then there exists N ∗∈K with N ∗≥M2 and f : M1 →N ∗fixing M0 such that
f[M1] ∩M2 = M0. Relabelling |N ∗| if necessary, without loss of generality, we may
assume that (f[|M1|] \ |M0|) ∩|M1| = ∅(move (f[|M1|] \ |M0|) to some other set
disjoint from both M1, N ∗, and replace N ∗by the induced structure, similar to
below). Define a bijective function g : |N ∗| →A where
(1) g(a) = f −1(a) if a ∈f[|M1|]
(2) g(a) = a if a ∈|N ∗| \ f[|M1|].
Note that if g fixes M0 as f fixes M0, so also g fixes M2 as M2 ∩f[M1] = M0.
Formally, A = |M1| ∪(|N ∗| \ f[|M1|]). The bijection g defines a structure N with
|N| = A where g : N ∗∼= N. By the isomorphism axioms of abstract classes, note
that N ∈K, g[f[M1]] = M1 ≤K N, and g[M2] = M2 ≤K N. So N is as desired.
□
The following example shows that, in the setting of AECs, DAP is a strictly
stronger property than AP.
Example 2.4. Let K = (K, ≤K) be the AC determined as follows:
(1) K is the class of all models M = (|M|, E) where E is an equivalence relation
on |M| such that each equivalence class of E has at most two elements
(2) ≤K is the submodel relation ⊆
It is not hard to see that this is an AEC with LS(K) = ℵ0, stable in all µ ≥ℵ0, and
satisfies AP, JEP, and NMM. However, the disjoint amalgamation property fails in
not only K, but in Kµ for every cardinal µ ≥ℵ0.
To see this, take M = (µ \ {1, 2}, E) where E0 has equivalence classes {i} for
i ∈|M| (all classes are singletons). For l = 1, 2, take Ml = (|M| ∪{l}, El) where El
has equivalence classes {0, l} and {i} for i ∈[3, µ) (that is, we added a new element
l to the class of 0). It is clear that M, M1, M2 ∈K and M ≤K Ml for l = 1, 2.
Supposing for contradiction M were a disjoint amalgamation base, by Lemma 2.3,
there would be a model N = (|N|, EN) ∈K with Ml ≤K N for l = 1, 2. But
then 0EN1 and 0EN2, meaning the equivalence class of 0 in N had at least three
elements, contradicting the definition of K.

Limit models of any limit length δ < λ+ exist in any λ-stable AEC.
Fact 2.6 ([GrVa06, 2.9, 2.12]). Let K be an AEC and λ ≥LS(K). Suppose Kλ
has AP. If ⟨Mi : i ≤λ⟩is a ≤K-increasing sequence in Kλ, and for all i < λ Mi+1
realises all types over Mi, then Mλ is universal over M0.
If K is also stable in λ ≥LS(K) with AP in Kλ, then any model M ∈Kλ has
a universal extension N ∈Kλ. Moreover, if δ < λ+ is limit, then for any M ∈Kλ
there exists a (λ, δ)-limit model N over M.
It is well known that limit models (over the same base) of the same cofinality of
length are isomorphic (over the base).
Fact 2.7 ([ShVi99, 1.3.6]). Let K be an AC where Kλ has AP. Let M, N1, N2 ∈Kλ
where Nl is a (λ, δl)-limit model over M for l = 1, 2. Suppose cf(δ1) = cf(δ2). Then
there is an isomorphism f : N1 ∼= N2 fixing M.
Furthermore, if Kλ has JEP, then given any N1, N2 ∈Kλ where Nl is a (λ, δl)-
limit model for l = 1, 2 (not necessarily over the same base), then there is an
isomorphism f : N1 ∼= N2.
The question of when limit models are isomorphic is an important one, and more
can be said under stronger assumptions (see Fact 2.43), but we save this for after
our discussion of towers.

When K is a nice sub-AC of an AEC but does not contain arbitrary unions, the
usual notion of universal continuity (or (≥ℵ0)-continuity in the notation above) is
less useful than the ‘universal continuity*’ defined originally in [BeMa, 3.2] (which is
equivalent when arbitrary unions of universal chains are in the AC). While writing
[Bea25] the author realised there is a minor missing assumption in [BeMa, 3.2],
which is that the types computed in the larger class are compatible with those
computed in the smaller class. We formalise this with the following definition.
Definition 2.13 ([Bea25, Definition 2.11]). Let K be an AC with sub-AC K′, both
with AP. We say K′ respects types from K if
(1) for all M ∈K′, ΦM : gSK′(M) →gSK(M) given by ΦM(gtpK′(a/M, N)) =

3. Main results
The goal of this section is to prove the main theorem:
Theorem 3.1. Assume Hypothesis 2.22. Assume M0, M1, M2 ∈K(λ,≥κ), and that
M0 ≤K Ml and al ∈Ml for l = 1, 2. Then there exist N ∈K(λ,≥κ) and fl : Ml →N
fixing M0 for l = 1, 2 such that gtp(fl(al)/f3−l[M3−l], N) ⌣-does not fork over M0
and f1[M1] ∩f2[M2] = M0. That is, ⌣↾K(λ,≥κ) satisfies disjoint non-forking
amalgamation.
In particular, every M0 ∈K(λ,≥κ) is a disjoint amalgamation base in Kλ.
Our argument is loosely inspired by the proof of [Vas19, 5.36].
The overall
strategy is as follows: we will show that we can form a reduced tower T 1 with
M0 at the bottom and M1 at the top such that the first singleton is a1. We then
‘amalgamate’ this with the tower T 2 = ⟨M0, M2⟩∧⟨a2⟩. By ‘amalgamate’, we mean
that we find a matrix of models where the leftmost column is given by T 1 and the
bottom row is given by the image of T 2 under some map f (see Figure 2). In fact,
calling the second column T ∗, we will have T 1 ◁(λ,≥κ) T ∗. The type of a1 over
f[M2] will not fork over M0 because of the tower ordering, and by amalgamating
the towers carefully using a modified version of Fact 2.34 (Lemma 3.5), we can
make sure that the type of f(a2) over M1 ⌣-does not fork over M0 also. So taking
N = Mα,1, f1 : M1 →N the inclusion map, and f2 = f : M2 →N, we have the
desired properties. In particular, disjointness follows from making the first tower
reduced (see Figure 2).
The brunt of the work when applying this strategy lies in building the tower T 1
(in particular, ensuring it is reduced), and making sure the amalgamation of towers
has the desired non-forking properties for a2. We can achieve this by mimicking the

Remark 3.2. It is worth making some comparison with [Vas19, 5.36], in particular
where our approach and theirs differ.
(1) Building the first tower T 1 with the necessary properties (in particular,
being reduced) is more difficult in our context - we summarise the problems
and our workarounds at the start of Subsection 3.2.
(2) [Vas19] assumes full categoricity, but while not stated explicitly, it ap-
pears the only reason this is used rather than the weaker λ-superstable
λ-symmetric assumptions of the rest of [Vas19, §5] is to get that every
M ∈Kλ is an amalgamation base (rather than just (λ, ≥ℵ0)-limit mod-
els). This was the basis of why Theorem 3.1 seemed plausible to the author
in our more general setting.
(3) In the proof of [Vas19, 5.36], the second tower T ′ (T 2 in our terminology) is
with extra work made to be reduced and of some limit length δ∗, witnessing

uses that T is reduced, you could instead take T ′ = ⟨M0, M2⟩∧⟨a2⟩as in
our argument, which simplifies the picture.

3.4. Disjoint amalgamation from a weaker relation. In this section we de-
scribe how under weaker assumptions, we can use analogous machinery to get dis-
joint amalgamation in a broader class of strictly stable AECs, at the sacrifice of
losing the non-forking of singletons. The proof is actually much shorter, though we
will have to establish the new setting briefly.
More precisely, we assume the underlying framework of [Bea25], which is identical
to Hypothesis 2.22, but with the uniqueness, extension, and non-forking amalga-
mation assumptions replaced by their ‘weak’ counterparts. First we introduce the
weakened form of non-forking amalgamation, which is essentially the usual notion
but where the non-forking is pushed down to a model M0 which the base of the
amalgamation M is a particular kind of limit model over.

Hypothesis 3.18. Let K be an AEC stable in λ, where Kλ has AP. Let ⌣be

Similar to before, we can build a theory of towers in this more general setting,
though we will call them weak towers to distinguish them from our other notion
of tower from Defintion 2.27. This theory is described in detail in [Bea25], but we
give an abridged overview here.
Notation 3.19. Given a well order I, define the well order I−2 as follows:
(1) if otp(I) is 0 or limit, I−2 = I
(2) if otp(I) = γ + 1 for some limit γ and i1 is the final element of I, I−2 =
I \ {i1} (with the restriction of the ordering of I).
(3) if otp(I) = α + 2 and i1, i2 are the last two elements of I, I−2 = I \ {i1, i2}
(with the restriction of the ordering of I).
That is, I−2 is I with the final two elements removed, if they exist.

We have one immediate application of Theorem 3.17 that does not satisfy the
hypotheses of Theorem 3.1.
Corollary 3.27. Suppose K is an AEC stable in λ ≥LS(K), that κ < λ+ is
regular, that θ ∈[κ, λ+) is regular. Suppose Kλ has AP, JEP, and NMM, and also
that λ-non-splitting in Kλ satisfies continuity, (≥κ)-local character, and (λ, θ)-
symmetry (see e.g. [Bea25, Definition 2.23]).
Then K(λ,≥κ) has disjoint non-forking amalgamation in K.
Proof. By the method of [Bea25, Corollary 4.1], λ-non-splitting satisfies Hypothesis
2.23 (which is identical to [Bea25, Hypothesis 3.3]), and therefore Hypothesis 2.22.
The result follows from Theorem 3.17.
□
As stated earlier, this result is stronger that Theorem 3.1 in the sense that our
relation has weaker assumptions, but weaker than Theorem 3.1 in that we have only
shown (λ, ≥κ)-limit models are disjoint amalgamation bases, without capturing any
information about the non-forking properties of singletons. The following seems the
most natural version of disjoint non-forking amalgamation in this ‘weaker’ setting:
Definition 3.28. Assume Hypothesis 3.18. We say ⌣satisfies weak disjoint non-
forking amalgamation if for all M0, M, M1, M2 ∈K(λ,≥κ) such that M is a (λ, ≥κ)-
limit model over M0, M ≤K Ml and al ∈Ml such that gtp(al/M, Ml) ⌣-does not
fork over M0, then there exist N ∈K(λ,≥κ) and fl : Ml →N fixing M such that
gtp(fl(al)/M3−l, N) ⌣-does not fork over M0 for l = 1, 2, and f1[M1]∩f2[M2] = M.
Remark 3.29. Note this is essentially (λ, θ)-weak disjoint amalgamation, with
the additional disjointness conclusion. Under Hypothesis 3.18, in light of Theorem
3.25(9), the definition would be equivalent if we added a θ parameter where cf(θ) ≥
κ and instead required M0 be a (λ, θ)-limit model over M∗.
Remark 3.30. Note given an independence relation with uniqueness and existence,
this is a weaker property than disjoint non-forking amalgamation: monotonicity
gives that the types ⌣-do not fork over M0, and after using disjoint non-forking
amalgamation, the conclusion follows from transitivity.
This leads to the following natural conjecture:
Question 3.31. Assume Hypothesis 3.18.
Does ⌣satisfy weak disjoint non-
forking amalgamation?


## Page 27


REFERENCES
27
We found that the proof of Theorem 3.1 breaks down at certain points when
using weak towers in place of towers and have thus been unable to answer Question
3.31.
Perhaps the most fundamental issue is that we would want the bottom the two
towers being amalgamated to be equal to M to get the correct intersection - but
then we cannot capture the non-forking of the singletons over M0 in the towers
themselves. Weak transitivity seems insufficient to get around this complication,
since the models in the reduced tower (the leftmost column) are not necessarily
universal extensions of one another (in fact, since the tower is reduced, intuitively
they will be very close to one another to guarantee the intersection property). With
this in mind, perhaps a modified version of towers would be necessary to answer
Question 3.31.
Remark 3.32. In fact, both Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.17 hold without the
assumptions of JEP and NMM in Kλ. If JEP fails, given M ∈Kλ, restrict to the
AEC KM of models which can be embedded into a model with M, as in [Bea25,
Definition 3.12]. All M1, M2 ∈K with M ≤K M1, M2 are in KM; the restriction
of ⌣to KM retains its properties in KM; and KM has JEP. So, we can prove the
result in KM instead.
Now we have JEP without loss of generality. Note that if NMM fails in Kλ, then
by JEP any (λ, ≥κ)-limit model is maximal. Thus all amalgamations are trivially
disjoint, and the non-forking properties follow from existence. So we can assume
NMM in Kλ holds without losing generality.
